stimulus: So, Tell Arvani. For a century the story was that the town died of drought — you'll still find that in older textbooks. But the sediment cores tell a different story: through the settlement's final decades, rainfall stayed right around the region's long-term average. Not a slow drying trend, not wild swings from wet to dry, and not some unusual wet period either — ordinary years, one after another. Which removes the easy answer. Now, the storage jars. Everyone assumed grain — big jars, farming town. But the residue analysis came back unambiguous: the large jars had mostly held olive oil, pressed right at the settlement — we have the crushing basins. Not barley from the surrounding fields, not wine hauled in from elsewhere, and no fish residues at all. This was a town producing oil, probably for exchange. What about Kessara, the neighbor? I bring it up for one reason: the team there has been using micro-stratigraphy and full flotation sampling — methods a generation newer than anything used at Arvani — and I want exactly that toolkit brought to our site. stimulus: Let's talk about the Serrat caldera, two thousand four to twelve. Start with the ground itself. The GPS and the radar agreed: the uplift sat squarely over the center of the caldera, and — this is the part that puzzled everyone — it went on climbing, millimeter by millimeter, long after the earthquake swarms had stopped. There was no sign of the ground settling back, no cycle of rise and fall, and the deformation was every bit as broad as the first reports said. Steady, quiet inflation. Then the gases. The chemistry wouldn't let you call it magma alone, and you couldn't pin it all on heated groundwater either — the emissions carried both signatures at once, magmatic and hydrothermal together, which points to a mixed source: magma degassing into an active water system. And these were not the tired gases of an old, cooling body; the ratios were fresh. Now, why did everyone take this so seriously? Because of the eighteen-sixties. The opening phase of that episode looked strikingly like what the instruments were now recording — the same quiet inflation, the same gas rise — and that episode, remember, ended in an eruption. Observers back then read the signs correctly, as it happens, and its deposits were quarried away long ago, useless for mapping anything. The resemblance was the whole alarm. Which brings us to the alert level. I'll be blunt: when it was raised in oh-eight, the instruments were saying nothing new that week. The newspapers, though, were saying plenty. No one could call the move late, and there was no protocol forcing anyone's hand. The pressure was coming from the public, and the committee moved with it.

stimulus: The Verrine Hours. Let's start with what the spectroscopy settled last spring: the blue is lapis, everywhere we looked — the Virgin's robe, yes, but even the little border sprays are lapis. There is no cheaper base layer under it; the lapis goes right down to the parchment, and there is no indigo at all, no azurite anywhere in the book. Now here is my larger point about this workshop, the point I want you to take away: what it used was governed by each patron's purse, not by any rule of the craft. A rich commission, and there is lapis in the margins; a modest one, and the same painters worked wonders with cheap blues. It was never about a house style of materials — and for the record, these compositions match no model book we know, nobody confuses these books with Arden work, and stylistically they kept pace with the newest fashions. It was the money. Which is exactly why I keep returning to the account books: the payments simply stop in the third year, mid-campaign, and that is why the last two gatherings sit unfinished. The accounts never name a single assistant, they don't itemize the pigments, frustratingly, and they won't give you dates precise enough to narrow production — but they do record that break in payment. So: is this Anselm's book? I say yes — but not for the reasons usually given. The faces, if anything, look like assistants' work, and the underdrawing is too varied to be one hand. But the page architecture — the layouts, those border systems — no one else in the region built pages that way, and every page sits comfortably within his working life.

stimulus: Marell Atoll, five years after cyclone Osea. The seedling survey came back this spring, and the pattern is odd: nearly everything new is strung along the debris lines — those windrows of wrack the storm left behind. Hardly any seedlings under the parent trees themselves, but along the wrack lines, dense little rows. And to be clear, there was no shortage of seedlings overall, and they were surviving the dry months just fine. Kanari recruitment hasn't collapsed — it has moved. Why? The imperial pigeons disperse the seed, and the follow-up work told us what changed. It isn't the vine — the feeding branches are clear; the vine never reached them. The rats we could rule out too: the exclosures made no difference. And fruiting still lines up with the breeding season the way it always has. No — the flocks are simply too small now. A crop that three hundred birds once cleared in a week hangs there, drops, and rots before the remaining dozens get to it. The storm surge then rakes the fallen fruit into the wrack lines — hence the pattern. Now, people always ask about the mainland kanari forests. I am not pointing to the mainland to say other animals could take over, nor to argue the problem stops at the shoreline, and I am certainly not proposing it as a source of birds. What I am asking is whether anything we learned in those forests transfers to an atoll at all — I doubt the comparison more each year. And yes, we are acting: a small trial, carrying fruit by hand past the surge zone, is already running on the island's two worst-hit stretches. Pigeon counts are still falling, so nobody is waiting on a rebound; we're not opposed to intervening — quite the opposite — and no one has put a translocation of birds on the table.

stimulus: Today, the Taruic vowel shift — and I want to use it to show how much you can squeeze out of very indirect evidence. Start with the vocabulary Taruic shares with its neighbor, Emel. The direction of borrowing isn't in doubt: Taruic into Emel — the cultural terms all run that way. And Emel's borrowed forms keep the old vowels. So the words crossed over before anything had shifted; the shift comes after the borrowing. Each of these words was borrowed once, and once only — there are no doubled forms. stimulus: The Adriatic storm-warning service. Begin with the wreck of the Stella Maris in December 1873 — two hundred and eleven lives. stimulus: Today, Fantin's dance suites — specifically the set of manuscript parts kept at Welden. Start with their condition, because it surprised everyone. These are not working copies. The corners are crisp, there are no performers' markings, no wax, and what little rubbing exists is uniform from the first suite to the last. The letter is the prize. Were these pieces for actual dancing? I say yes, and the scores tell you so themselves: the repeat schemes fit the surviving choreographies figure for figure, and that holds for every movement, first to last. The tempo markings are perfectly danceable, and the court ledger tells us nothing either way. Finally, the missing second-violin book. The editors will not invent the line themselves, and they refuse to print the suites with a hole in the texture. The rumored amateur copy has never been traced. Just the mixing. Now, the spike of seventeen sixty-eight. The price series built from these ledgers is stark: the rise appears everywhere at once. Coast, uplands, market towns — within days of one another, which for that century is simultaneity. The inland towns did not lead, the ports did not lead, and nothing hopped from town to town; there was no sequence to find. And the partners? At the height, the letters show them carrying. Their ships spent the crisis hauling other houses' grain for freight fees — steady money, no exposure. They never sold out early to watch from shore, timber never tempted them, and the city never engaged them to buy on its account. Carriers, by choice. Which leaves the old story of a merchant ring withholding grain. I dismiss it, on arithmetic alone: no ring could have warehoused enough to move prices beyond a week. stimulus: When Gravenstad pulled down its walls, the council took forty years over it — and that, I will argue, was wisdom. stimulus: TW Corvi's disk, and the dark ring everyone argues about. Some history first. stimulus: The Tarei valley bands. The looms are busy — everyday cloth is made in every hamlet, and it is woven in the valley itself, not bought in from downriver. But the marriage patterns are another matter: those designs have been retired. Nobody has set one on a loom in two generations. The old bands still move through marriage payments; no new ones join them. Weaving lives; that one repertoire is closed. Now, the district officer's inventory of nineteen-oh-two. Its value is a fact people overlook: it lists bands held by families three districts away. The things had traveled far beyond the valley before any ethnographer arrived. That is all I want from it — it records no prices and no livestock equivalents, it had nothing to do with taxation, since the officer compiled it for a museum, and every pattern it names can be matched to a surviving band. How is a band's worth judged? Our fieldwork was unambiguous: by the hand. Elders roll the cloth between finger and thumb, and tightness is everything. A band's pedigree counts for little — nobody we asked cared much who wove a piece — no motif outranks another, and a new band, well woven, stands above a darkened old one. Finally, Marovic. Handle his monograph with tongs. On the loom, on technique, he is exact; we can verify him knot for knot. On exchange he matches nothing we recorded. His informants, the elders insist, dealt with him honestly, and what he described was no passing fashion of his decade. The failure was his own, and it sits squarely in the exchange chapters.

stimulus: The Lay of Ansfrid survives in one manuscript, the Stavenow codex, so start there. Those marginal glosses were long romanticized — generations of readers, layers of hands. The paleography says otherwise. One scribe, one ink, one sitting: the glosses were already in the exemplar, and the scribe copied margin and column together as a single package. They don't touch the dialect anywhere, and they are commentary proper, not any owner's index for finding passages. Now the famous lament. My point is blunt: the original poet didn't write it. The vocabulary shifts, the hero's byname changes form — a continuator supplied the whole section, probably within a generation. It matches no school exercise we can identify, it borrows from no chronicle — people have looked hard — and it plays the genre's conventions absolutely straight. Why do I keep citing Brandt's edition? Not her dating, which nobody builds on anymore, and hardly for access — few students ever read her; the translation went out of print decades ago. She worked from the Stavenow codex alone, to her credit. But she invented the stanza numbering, and every article you will ever cite still uses it. Finally: composed for performance? Yes — and the rhymes settle it for me. Those chime patterns only work aloud; on the page they read as errors. stimulus: Twenty-two years of banding data on the scrub wren — let's see what it actually says. Why do I keep bringing up Charby Island? One reason. The Charby wrens all descend from a release in nineteen fifty-four that was written down bird by bird, so their ancestry is known completely — priceless for the genetic work. The island survey used different methods entirely, so it is no comparison group; the species was first described on the mainland; and no storm has ever knocked the Charby population down. Next, the recapture records on the older males. Their territories did not sit still, but they didn't wander toward the wetland either, and nobody swapped ground with a neighbor. The same males returned to the same centers, and each season the boundary drew in a little — slow, steady shrinkage, year over year. Third — students always ask — why so few females in the records? Not tag loss; the tags stay on females just as well. Trapping runs year-round, nesting months included, and the radio-tagged females almost never cross into the reserve next door. The real issue is placement: the trap lines follow the ridgetops, and females spend their days down in the gullies. Finally, Vasquez, who reads winter flocking as a response to predators. I'd say she has it inverted: the flocks assemble first, and the hawks find them — flocks by October, hawks by November, in her own data. Remember, the hawks were here before any record we have, the pattern is identical coastal and inland, and these counts come from open scrub with no feeders anywhere near.

stimulus: The Salvera chart. Perrin argued it was a display piece, never meant for the deck of a ship, and I have come around to his view. Someone added the entire northern edge long after the maker was done; nothing else on the chart uses that ink batch. Why the Ferrandin atlas? Not for errors — it shares none of ours — its preface names nobody, and the harbor argument collapsed years ago; the silting cannot be dated. But the Ferrandin sits in its original dated binding: the one fixed point among all these undated charts. Last, the place-names in two languages. This is not a compiler splicing sources, and the second language was not added under new rulers — both sets are in the maker's own hand, first pass. The maker worked in a port where both tongues crossed the same counter, and the chart talks the way his harbor talked. Nothing rare is preserved; both dialects are documented elsewhere.

stimulus: The Tarveny hoard — six hundred silver pieces and not one small denomination. The tempting stories fail. The find was excavated under supervision from the first spade, so nobody skimmed the change; the mint recalled nothing in those decades — the withdrawal lists survive and are empty — and small coins circulated freely in the region; site finds around Tarveny are full of them. No: the small stuff was bronze, and the Tarveny soil is aggressive — acid, waterlogged — and it eats bronze completely. The little coins were there; they dissolved. Now the die study. For the commonest type we expected a tight cluster. Instead the coins scatter across an enormous number of dies, and the dies almost never link. You cannot build a chain, so forget any minting order, and every die is official work — not one local imitation in the lot. Money gathered from wide circulation. The second hoard, across the river — I bring it up for the pot. It came out of the ground still in its jar, packing intact, the very context our hoard lost; mind you, its recovery was every bit as hurried as ours. Its latest coins run decades apart from ours, and its contents mirror the first hoard type for type. Finally, Teodorescu reads Tarveny as a soldier's pay. I do not buy it. Coins worn to slickness lying beside mint-fresh pieces are what a household accumulates across two generations; pay comes fresh. The total lands between every pay grade we know, the pieces show no sorting by weight, and the corrosion is uniform: one deposit, buried once.

stimulus: A logging road opened along the Vireno ridge five years ago, and we have followed the macaque groups through it. Start with the sleeping cliffs. We expected desertion. Instead, all four cliffs stayed in use — including the one nearest the roadbed — and the groups kept their old rotation among them, no cliff more crowded than before. Not once in five years was a group found bedding in the canopy. What changed was the clock: groups that settled at dusk now come in well after dark. My colleague Deren reads this as predator response — leopards moving along the new corridor. I think he has it backwards. The wariness he treats as the driver is itself a product of the disturbance — jumpy animals look predator-pressed. The model's pedigree is not the issue — it was built on forest species in forest much like this — but the evidence for it is thinner than for either rival account, and it never fit even our first season's data. A caution about the follow records. Two teams shadowed two groups in parallel, so same-day comparisons exist. Both seasons fell in the same fruiting year, and every ear notch stayed legible to the end. The real limit is habituation: the boldest groups tolerated observers within weeks; the shyest never quite did, and are thin in the record accordingly. The forestry department acted on the report: within a month, crews were setting out rows of quick-growing figs along the bare roadcut. stimulus: Marthe Dole's notebooks, and what the canal company's toll ledgers add. One entry matters most: a payment to M. Dole, for computing the cuttings — she was paid to calculate, not merely to carry a chain, and that is the whole of my point with the ledgers. They record no purchases of instruments, they place her on the western line — the very stretch where the notebooks later surfaced — and the company archive survives virtually complete; the fire of 1774 never reached the ledger room. Dating the pages was harder. The watermarks tell us nothing — that paper stock was in production for fifty years. The ink is uniform from the first page to the last: one sustained campaign of writing, not several. And the notebooks mention no bridge, no lock, no datable structure at all. What settled it was the binding: nineteenth-century work, far younger than the pages, and once it was set aside, the exposed sewing pattern matched an atelier active only in the 1730s. Now, Odile's objection — that Dole's shortcut fails on steep ground. I accept it. The notebooks flag their own hill pages as doubtful, in Dole's hand. The two hill surveys that survive miss badly against modern measurement, contemporaries used the rival tables on steep ground and got it right, and commissions of the period did hire the shortcut for upland work — the failure is real. After her death, the notebooks went to a schoolmaster at Aubrec, who taught from them for thirty years. They were never separated, their whereabouts are documented in every decade since, and Dole left no heirs.

stimulus: The Ansel banner. The fiber and dye analysis gave one discovery: the reds are two different dyestuffs — madder in the original field, a later synthetic in the restitched panels. A repair campaign, then, generations after the weaving. Both reds are true dyes carried in the thread; nothing was brushed onto the finished cloth. The madder is the local strain, from dye-works in the banner's own district, and the colorants show no drift from purple — this red was always red. Why dwell on the 1968 treatment? Not because it haunts us: the backing came away cleanly in 1994 and took the adhesive with it. Not for its photographs, which show the border exactly as the cloth shows it today. And its paperwork never once mentions the discoloration. I describe it because it won a prize — admired, published, imitated — and no conservator alive would defend it now. That is how fast this field moves. The trial cleaning of one corner, next. The stains came away evenly, but the water betrayed us — a tide line crept in as the corner dried, and only a second pass chased it out. Fibers from under the grime tested no different from the exposed areas, and the cleaned corner drapes as softly as the rest. Last, the parish question. There is nothing to debate: the 1961 loan agreement lets the parish recall the banner at will, and preference does not come into it. The church, climate-controlled for years, stays dry the year round; the parish has promised nothing about display; and my lab was never consulted in the dispute.

stimulus: The Sella valley, and Ovel's cylinders. The winter singing evenings first: their real work was survival. By the nineties emigration had emptied farm after farm, and the evenings kept the ballads sung once the households that carried them were gone. No invention of Ovel's day, either — parish complaints about the gatherings run back to the 1740s. Nor did they blend anything together: each farm's version stayed its own — Ovel could tell a Brenholt text from a Vasse by the third line. And print never got in — she found not one broadside in the whole valley. Second, the quarrel over putting the cylinders online. One fact recasts it: the singers' own descendants petitioned for the release, three families in writing. You cannot settle it from Ovel's contracts, which say nothing about publication either way; the archive consulted far beyond the collector's estate; and the wax is in excellent condition, so the cylinders' state is no part of the argument. Third, notebooks beside wax — the striking thing is absence: dozens of songs entered in her hand were never recorded at all; wax was dear, and she rationed it. Where both survive, they match word for word; her texts carry every refrain the wax carries; and every singer she lists is a distinct voice on the cylinders. Last, the customs post at the valley mouth — a boundary and nothing else: past it the Sella ballads stop and the coastal stock takes over. Its ledgers record goods, not travelers; its officers never sang for her; and both her visits are dated to the day in her own diary.

stimulus: Brenwick's water mains began bursting in the winter of 1871; the inquiry that followed is our subject. Its tests told a simple story: every failed pipe came from a single casting run — the foundry's autumn pour, brittle across all samples — while pipe from other runs in the same streets never failed. The trenches sat in natural gravel that had never been disturbed; the new engines were metered, and pressure never rose past the old maximum; and the bursts came in August as often as in January — so much for frost. Notice, though, the inquiry's stamina: chartered for six months, it sat for five years, long after the public anger had died away — that persistence is the real lesson. Its yard tests were matched deliberately to buried conditions; not one gauge of its own went into the ground — the panel worked from testimony; and the laborers were examined as suspects. Why the rival company across the river? Rates. A decade of undercutting had poisoned everything, and the city would not fund repairs whose cost would surface in that rate war — that is why the money stalled. No one from the rival sat on the panel, the rival never bid for the works — the city itself absorbed them in the end — and the report went to the printers on schedule. The recommendations? Hamburg and Turin wrote them into practice within five years; at home they were never written into any code of the period, not even for the new districts, and when steel mains arrived the testing rules carried over unchanged.

stimulus: Madariaga spent three years inside the Solana wholesale market, and the study still shapes how we think about informal order. His conclusion on the prized corner positions: seniority. Years on the floor decided who moved up when a pitch fell vacant — an order everyone could recite and nobody had written down. Not kinship: sons ranked behind longer-tenured newcomers, and the best pitches did not run in families. Not chance: he hunted for a lottery and found the traders laughing at the idea. Not hidden favors either: the fee books enter every transfer, dated, each matching the seniority queue exactly. Now, the months behind a stall of his own. Readers long puzzled over the silence in his field notes; the explanation is homely — minding the stall left no hand free to write, and the gap is exactly those months. The committee never admitted him; the account before and after keeps its cool distance perfectly; and the pre-dawn auctions he never saw — his stock came by consignment at midday. Bahn's objection, that the traveling vendors are missing, I concede: the census sheets stop at the permanent stalls. And Bahn's list was compiled in the study's final year. But the matters at issue were the fixed positions, where the travelers held no claim, and the omission leaves the central claim standing. The move to the new hall in 1954 is the coda: within a year the surrounding streets held more stalls than the hall did, the city's numbered plan inside was ignored from the first week, the seniority order never re-formed indoors, and not one dispute reached the municipal courts.

stimulus: Vaissalu's drawings, set beside the stones that still stand. He drew some forty memorials in the seventeen nineties; nine of those stones survive. The comparison isn't flattering. Two things he's innocent of, mind: where a stone had flaked, he leaves a gap, honestly blank; and his churchyard attributions hold up wherever we can test them. How did I come to this? The parsonage at Kolgama. I catalogued its library as a student, one wet summer, and there was Rennik's sketchbook. The dating quarrel now. Hallik dates the group later than the years carved on it. I'd narrow that. One carver, the Ansu master, worked late, and his pieces colour how the rest get read; I would not extend that to the group. The formulas are common regional ones, older than any printed model I know, and the stone there weathers fast, so I don't rest a case on weathering. Twenty-odd stones are unlocated. We won't print a text nobody has seen on the stone, and they stay in the corpus volume, marked missing. A handlist goes to the county museums; some may sit unrecognized in a storeroom. stimulus: Sarvela's beetles — eleven thousand pins, and questions the specimens cannot settle. Start with the coastal meadows. The literature says Kepsara's ground beetle vanished around nineteen ten. Rehepapp takes that at face value. Ilves says the older records are misidentified relatives, since the sister species was not split off until the fifties and much of the coastal literature predates the split — a fair worry. The post-war sweeping in the meadows themselves amounts to two afternoons. What thins out around nineteen ten is the collecting, not the beetle. The nineteen-oh-four auction catalogue. One copy carries a pencil note naming the buyer, whose heirs gave us the material — that is how the chain closes. Its lot descriptions run to a line each, too thin to match a box against, the prices in it are steep for the day, and the cabinet it lists came to the museum with the rest. The labels. There is no pencil under the ink; one hand wrote the coastal labels and its abbreviations don't vary; the oldest hand is Sarvela's own, from his school years. What the writing shows is a nineteen-thirties re-curation: a good many labels rewritten, the old spellings quietly modernized. Next: not re-pinning, the pins stay where Sarvela put them; not sequencing, we won't cut them; not the traded duplicates, Vaher published that list years ago. The mites that ride on these beetles — nobody has looked.

stimulus: Turvaste — three parish volumes, and the crisis years at their centre. What the registers show is not a parish dying evenly. The burials fall heavily on households that had arrived within the previous decade, cottagers, hired men, families off the road, while the long-settled farms came through comparatively lightly. Not departure: the town lists show no bulge of arrivals from here in those years. Not two waves either — the burials run in one long swell. And the hamlets and the church village lost at much the same rate. Now, the entries. Halliste built a good deal on the cause column, and Piir on the lists at the back, both worth having: each says the register shapes what we think we see. But the cause column runs right through the crisis, and stillbirths are entered in the main sequence. The entries give a name and a farm, and leave the messenger out. The close reading shows the clerk wrote up several days at a time, so the day-by-day dating everyone quotes is ours, not the parish's. The eighteen-eighties rebinding. The margins came through it uncut, no bill for the work has been found, and the covers went back on plain. What did happen is that a few leaves from the parish upriver were bound in by mistake, and nobody caught it until the nineteen thirties. Next? Not the rent rolls, Turvaste's burned in the eighteen forties. Not the neighbours, whose registers are in poor shape. Grain prices are already in the appendix of my first article. I want the slow method: reconstituting a sample of households in full.

Kuivalinn hall came down in nineteen sixty-one. What survives is Rebasmaa's notebooks, eleven recordings, and Nommiste's drawings. Rebasmaa measured with pistol shots fired from the stage, logged position by position across two evenings. He had asked the mill to send workers in to fill the seats; the mill declined, so the hall stood empty for both sittings. What he entered are the single readings themselves, not averages; no cards stand behind them. The hall was renovated in fifty-four and he did not go back, so that book holds one campaign, not two.

Was the sound as fine as its reputation? I think so: a modern designer would still envy the measured values. The memoirists came late and added little. The resident orchestra was a middling band that toured to no acclaim. And these figures are not the long reverberation that period taste supposedly prized - they are short and defined.

Now the recordings. Cleaned digitally, they can anchor a computed model of the room, which no drawing on its own could support. The players were shifted between takes with no note kept, so the discs will not fix anybody's placement, and the room's contribution sits well above the surface noise once cleaned. The studio discs are a different decade and a different orchestra.

Next, then. Rebuilding a length of that wall at full scale was costed and is beyond us; the museum will mount its exhibition without our help; the local press we have read through already. Nommiste's smaller hall at Harmavere still stands, and we will measure it as our stand-in.

Soorna is a small brown lake with a deep archive: Virkland's notebooks from the eighteen nineties, the fishermen's association minute-books, and our series since eighty-eight.

The minute-books first: they settle a dating problem. The association paid Virkland's boatman by the day, and the payments are dated, fixing the seasons his notebooks leave vague. Their other contents are thin. The net-fouling complaints are undated grumbles; the argument about the springs names no location, being a quarrel over payment; and the catch was weighed at the landing for two years before the practice lapsed.

Virkland's transparency readings against ours. They scatter too widely to carry a trend - to his credit the notebooks say why, listing wind and cloud for each cast. The scatter is not a steady offset. His figures run deeper on some days and shallower on others, in the bays and on the open water alike, and matching him week for week does not tighten the cloud.

Kivrand argues the darkening began centuries before the first surveys. I reject that. Those proxies move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever colour the water is - and Soorna's level has shifted. So I am not dating the onset a little later than Kivrand does, I am not pushing it further back on the pollen and charcoal, and I am not calling the darkening periodic either.

The minute-books first: they settle a dating problem. The association paid Virkland's boatman by the day, and the payments are dated, fixing the seasons his notebooks leave vague. Their other contents are thin. The net-fouling complaints are undated grumbles; the argument about the springs names no location, being a quarrel over payment; and the catch was weighed at the landing for two years before the practice lapsed.

Virkland's transparency readings against ours. They scatter too widely to carry a trend - to his credit the notebooks say why, listing wind and cloud for each cast. The scatter is not a steady offset. His figures run deeper on some days and shallower on others, in the bays and on the open water alike, and matching him week for week does not tighten the cloud.

So I am not dating the onset a little later than Kivrand does, I am not pushing it further back on the pollen and charcoal, and I am not calling the darkening periodic either.

stimulus:
Kaldevere's garden, laid out in the seventeen nineties, and the question that comes first: was it Nurmsaar's? The design is his; the hand shows in the sweep of the approach. But I doubt he came. The plans travelled by post, and were adapted on site by whoever held the spade. The estate books enter no payment for a visit; his pupil's planting lists, which Harm compares with the beds, are a poor match; and the family were naming Nurmsaar in their own letters within two years of the digging, not a generation after.

Now the drawings against the ground. Harm reads the showpiece drawing as a tidied presentation piece, symmetrical on paper and loose in the soil, and I would believe that elsewhere. Here the bed edges we dug out in ninety-four sit where the drawing puts them, foot for foot, through the first campaign. Then it was set aside within a decade, as taste turned. The same sheet governs the park and the walled ground alike, and there is no rival drawing to braid it with.

The nursery invoices. Substitutions run right through them: Parnaste sent hardier kinds than the ones ordered. They date the water garden where the guidebooks do; they are made out to the steward; and the estate's own nursery supplied little beyond seed.

Tiidema's letter-book, last. It is a thin thing - a handful of letters, there are no blotting pages bound in, and his famous quarrel is not in it. What it does is show him at Kaldevere from boyhood, against the story that he was fetched from abroad.

stimulus: Trelundy infirmary and its weighing scheme. The dispenser's ledger first: it is a costing book. Extra diet, coals, the man's own hours, priced week by week; the total ran heavy enough that the governors twice set the scheme down for debate, and twice let it stand. Occupancy you get elsewhere: bed numbers come from the matron's returns. There are marginal notes, granted, haggling over the price of oatmeal. We date the break from the governors' minutes; the ledger runs unbroken through those years. The weighing itself. Physicians read the charts as a record of recovery. The ward staff had quite other ends in view: Friday's figures settled who could be put to work on the ward. The scale came in with a physician in the house's first month, and the kitchen inspections start twenty years later. Someone asked whether the balance was swapped — it was the same beam throughout. And the weighing did fix the shape of the week; true, though it is not my point. Maderwyn re-read the registers. Weight and length of stay track each other far more loosely than the reports of the day claimed. Winter and summer intakes gained at much the same rate. The gains scatter across quarter-ounces. The attendants' books disagree constantly rather than running alike. Rostrellick says the weighing shaped admission. His notes come from the eighteen sixties, a generation after the weighing began. Subscribers nominated, certainly, though the house physician struck names off the nomination lists. Until the admission registers are worked through, our papers cannot settle it — and I am withholding judgment on both ends.

The staff, meanwhile, got their instructions on printed slips, weekly. The archive is being catalogued. When that is done we shall see how the labour was shared out: each editor marked the material in his own ink, and those marks are on the slips still. Cut entries went with the proofs, and the proofs were pulped. The packets were opened by a clerk who kept the slips and burned the wrappers. Morgelly's studio ledger — Threlmoor, thirty years of sittings.

Pricing first. Across the square, Ivestead charged one fee for the sitting however many prints went out; Morgelly charged by the print. Ivestead's sitting stood a shilling below Morgelly's, and a group paid that same shilling again. His fee rose twice in twenty years, both times when he took larger premises. One of you had read that he discounted for regulars. His book gives the same figure for a stranger and for a man on his fourth sitting.

Chelvern says the ledger was written up afterwards, for show. I don't accept it. The ink shifts from entry to entry, the way a book kept daily will; the hand is his throughout, which tells us who wrote it, not when. The earliest volume shows the same ink shifts as the later ones. So: not an open question but a settled one — the ink changes at the entry.

Now, the plate makers' price lists. His exposures hold at about the same length right through the change of plates, and his invoices are bound into the back of the same ledger. The interest is not what he bought but what he sold on: the counter trade in plates and chemicals brought him more than the camera work did.

Which leaves the light. The handbook figures reach his pages a good decade after the journals printed them. He opens up a stop for children; past that, the settings answer the sky. It won't date his prints — half the sittings go unnamed — but knowing his habits, it reads as an instrument.

The measured mile off Aberwynt. In eighteen ninety-four a coal company put a pier across the sight line from the northern beacon, and the course had to be shifted a mile down the coast and surveyed afresh. The navy paid for the beacons and the navy paid to move them. Porthlenny's figures do sit a touch high, but the two grounds were surveyed to one standard and convert cleanly. And the timings came off the ship's own stopwatches, not from the shore huts.

Now, the yard papers, catalogued last winter. What I expect from them is the post survey: how far the marker posts had drifted from the distance the charts gave them. The Penvorran's propellers are in her completion book — the pair she carried into service. Her draught was read off the marks that morning and both sides signed for it. And the sister ship was six months from launching.

Nansveor charges the fleet with inflating trial speeds. I go part way with him. The export figures run high, by a knot and a half, and that was not an error in the current allowance but a decision taken ashore. The home trials come out straight, year after year.

Coal returns, finally. Ships tried in the winter months returned higher figures than those tried in summer. One of you suggested the stokers: sort the returns by stokehold and they scatter less than they do by ship. Trial-day burning sits above what the same ships used on passage. Two yards did return in bushels, and the clerk converted those before the tables were made up.
